Advice everyone can follow.
Our class planned a wellbeing afternoon for younger pupils. We first thought about a fast running game, but our teacher asked us to choose activities that different children could enjoy. We made three stations: a quiet drawing table, a gentle garden walk and a place to ask the school nurse questions. I helped at the walk. Before starting, I said, “You should stay with our group and tell an adult if you need to stop.” A boy called Max looked worried. He said he was not good at running. I explained that we were walking, not racing, and that nobody had to be the fastest. He began to relax. Halfway round the garden, another pupil said her foot hurt. I did not try to decide what was wrong. I told our teacher, who stayed with her and arranged help. The rest of us waited together. After the walk, Max chose the drawing table. He made a picture of the garden and showed it to me. At the end, our teacher asked what had worked well. I said the best advice was easy to follow and helped people ask for support. We did not need to turn every activity into a competition.
